claims.text: Thermal exposure within service conditions triggers a nucleation-and-growth transformation in the initially metastable Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The thermally induced transformation produces Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The initial state is a homogeneous solid solution with uniformly distributed constituent elements and minimal intermetallic phases.
High configurational entropy maintains the homogeneous solid solution in the initial metastable state.
Thermal exposure activates diffusion and causes Mg atoms and associated reactive species to aggregate.
Mg-containing intermetallic compounds form along grain boundaries or within the matrix.
Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have a tendency to contain complex or intermetallic precipitates.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes Mg and possibly other reactive species from the matrix.
Matrix Mg is needed to form a continuous, stable protective oxide or passivation film.
Mg depletion reduces the matrix's capacity to generate a protective oxide or passivation film.
The reduced protective-film-forming capacity degrades corrosion resistance.
The reduced protective-film-forming capacity degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit more detectable intermetallic phases and phase segregation than the initial state.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit higher oxidation weight gain or thicker, non-protective oxide scales than the initial state.
Thermally aged samples will exhibit increased corrosion rates or lower electrochemical impedance than the initial state.
The initial homogeneous metastable state has relatively superior corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The transformation becomes significant above approximately 600 degrees Celsius or after exposure long enough for diffusion and precipitation.
Below the relevant temperature and time thresholds, the metastable state remains substantially retained.
Precipitation kinetics and morphology depend on processing parameters and alloy composition.
A same-batch comparison between an unaged control and a thermally aged sample can test the proposed transformation and property-loss pathway.
